hook_n1: One nation once ruled a sixth of all the land on Earth.
hook_n2: Not Rome. Not Persia. A nation of herders, from the open steppe.
hook_n3: Barely a million people. Yet they toppled empires of tens of millions, one by one.
hook_n4: How was that even possible? The answer wasn't swords, or horses. It was a single number.
hook_n5: The number ten. And this is the story of the man who used it to swallow the world.
c1_01: Around 1162, on the Mongolian steppe, a minor tribal chief had a son. His name was Temüjin.
c1_02: When Temüjin was nine, his father Yesügei picked out a bride for him, and rode home alone.
c1_03: Along the way, his old enemies, the Tatars, recognized him. And they slipped poison into his food.
c1_04: With the chief dead, his tribe simply left. His mother Hoelun and her children were stranded in the middle of the steppe.
c1_05: They dug up wild roots and caught fish, just to stay alive.
c1_06: But the world wasn't done with him. The rival Taichiud captured him and locked a wooden collar on his neck.
c1_07: Yesügei's boy… Keep him alive. For now.
c1_08: One night, he escaped into a river.
c1_09: A searcher came closer, torch in hand. And then… he saw him.
c1_10: The man said nothing. He just turned, and walked on past.
c1_11: Temüjin never forgot him. Repay every kindness, repay every betrayal. That became his rule for life.
c2_01: As a young man, Temüjin kept his childhood promise and married Börte.
c2_02: Soon after, Merkit raiders struck in the night and carried Börte off.
c2_03: Years before, Yesügei had stolen his own bride, Hoelun, from a Merkit man. Now the Merkits took their revenge on his son's wife.
c2_04: Temüjin had no army. All he had left was a black sable coat, part of Börte's dowry.
c2_05: He took that coat to Toghrul, khan of the Keraites, and his father's sworn brother.
c2_06: My father's sworn brother is a father to me. Please, accept this coat.
c2_07: I'll gather your scattered people, and bring your wife back to you.
c2_08: Toghrul was among the most powerful khans on the steppe. He called in Jamukha, Temüjin's childhood sworn brother, and together they raised tens of thousands of horsemen.
c2_09: Temüjin had no army. But he had his father's old loyalties. And those became his first army.
c2_10: The three struck the Merkit camp by night.
c2_11: In the chaos, Temüjin shouted Börte's name. She knew his voice, ran to him out of the darkness, and seized his horse's reins.
c2_12: Afterward, the two sworn brothers shared a camp for a year and a half.
c2_14: The steppe belongs to those of noble blood.
c2_15: Your father doesn't matter. Only this: are you loyal, and can you fight?
c2_16: Nobles flocked to Jamukha, herders and slaves to Temüjin. Eventually, the sworn brothers turned their blades on each other.
c2_17: Around 1187, they met in battle at Dalan Baljut. Temüjin was badly beaten.
c2_18: Jamukha, it is said, boiled his prisoners alive in cauldrons.
c2_19: But that cruelty backfired. Terrified people abandoned Jamukha, the winner, and flocked to Temüjin, the loser.
c2_20: In 1201, Temüjin fought the Taichiud. Then an arrow flew out of the woods, and brought down Temüjin's horse.
c2_21: As the battle turned, the archer fled into the forest. But Temüjin's men caught him and dragged him back.
c2_22: Everyone assumed he was a dead man. Then the archer spoke first.
c2_24: If you kill me, / my blood will stain only a palm's breadth of earth. / But if you spare me, / for the Khan I will cleave deep waters, and shatter hard stone.
c2_25: An enemy hides what he has done. / You did not. / You are a man worth keeping.
c2_26: From this day, your name is Jebe, / which means arrow.
c2_27: Around then, a blacksmith's son named Subutai joined him too. Remember these two names. Together, they would be the first to rip into Europe.
c2_28: After that, nothing could stop him. In 1202, he crushed the Tatars who had poisoned his father. In 1203, Toghrul, the old ally who betrayed him. In 1204, the Naiman, the great power of the west.
c2_29: Jamukha held out longest, until his own men bound him and dragged him in. Temüjin executed the traitors first.
c2_30: Jamukha asked for only one last thing: to be allowed to die without shedding his blood.
c2_31: Temüjin granted his old sworn brother that last wish.
c2_32: In 1206, every tribe of the steppe knelt before one man. And the name he took was Genghis Khan.
c3_02: So Genghis Khan rebuilt the army from the ground up. And the key was the number ten.
c3_03: Ten soldiers made one unit. / In a modern army, that's roughly a squad.
c3_04: Ten of those units made a hundred men, / about the size of a company.
c3_05: Ten of those hundreds made a thousand men, / roughly a battalion.
c3_06: And ten of those thousands made ten thousand, / a unit to match a modern division.
c3_07: The Mongols called this ten-thousand-man unit a tumen.
c3_08: So why was this so powerful? There are four reasons.
c3_09: One: speed. To move ten thousand men, an order only had to pass down four times. And no officer ever had to manage more than ten people. With ten, you know every face, every name, every bad habit.
c3_10: Two: the tribes were mixed on purpose. Sworn enemies were put in the same unit.
c3_11: At first, of course, they bristled.
c3_12: But share a tent, share your meals, / fight the same enemy, and things change.
c3_13: Loyalty now went not to an old chief, / but to the nine men beside you.
c3_14: Switching units was forbidden too. The penalty was death.
c3_15: Three: collective punishment. Carpini, a European friar who visited the Mongols, wrote that if even one or two men in a ten fled, all ten were executed.
c3_16: Run, and the nine friends beside you die for it. So nobody ran.
c3_17: Four: it split apart easily. Need a thousand men? Send one unit of a thousand. Need twenty thousand? Send two tumens. Same structure, same behavior, anywhere. That's how the Mongols could strike on several fronts at once.
c3_18: So how did they train? By hunting. Tens of thousands of riders formed a giant ring across the plains, and over several weeks drove the animals toward the center. If the ring broke, the officer responsible for that stretch was punished.
c3_19: How to surround, / how to coordinate signals, / how to wait. They learned every bit of it on the hunt.
c3_20: The Mongols' deadliest trick came from the hunt too. / The feigned retreat.
c3_21: First, the Mongol front line engages the enemy, / then turns and runs, as if terrified.
c3_22: Convinced it has won, the enemy breaks formation and gives chase. / Fast horsemen race ahead while slow foot soldiers fall behind, / and the enemy's line stretches long and thin.
c3_23: And right then, / Mongol wings hidden behind the hills burst out and wrap around the stretched-out enemy from the sides. / The fleeing front line wheels its horses around.
c3_24: Like animals driven by hunters, / the enemy is trapped in arrows flying from every side.
c3_25: Europe would one day pay dearly to learn this trick.
c3_26: The last secret was the horse. / Every Mongol soldier rode with three or four horses in tow.
c3_27: When his horse tired, / he switched to a fresh one at full gallop. / The horses rested, but the army never stopped.
c3_28: They also kept relay stations along the roads, / with fresh horses waiting. / Drop off a tired mount, jump on a new one, and ride straight on.
c3_29: And no worries about fodder either. / Wherever they went, the endless steppe fed their horses.
c3_30: While other armies crawled along, hauling carts of grain and hay for their horses, / the Mongols rode with almost nothing.
c3_31: A day's march for the enemy, / the Mongols covered in half a day. And suddenly, there they were.
c4_01: Now Genghis Khan looked south, to the richest land on Earth: China. Its northern half belonged to the Jin dynasty, which had spent generations turning the steppe tribes against each other, and tormenting them.
c4_02: For over a thousand years, China had feared the northern steppe. / Riders would sweep in, plunder, / and vanish like the wind.
c4_03: The Great Wall was built to stop exactly them. / And yet the Jin, safe behind that wall, / had once been hunters who came down from the forests beyond it.
c4_04: But first, he skipped the Jin and struck Western Xia, on their flank.
c4_05: In 1209, the Mongols besieged the Western Xia capital, and broke open a riverbank to flood the city.
c4_06: The dike burst, and the water…
c4_07: poured straight into the Mongol camp.
c4_08: This is what happens when people who've never built a wall / try to attack one.
c4_09: But the Mongols didn't leave. / They kept the city ringed, layer upon layer.
c4_10: Xia begged the Jin for help, / but the Jin emperor turned away, saying it paid to let enemies fight each other.
c4_11: Alone, the city of Xia began to run out of food.
c4_12: In the end, Xia gave up a princess and tribute, and bowed its head. / Now his back was safe.
c4_13: In 1211, it was finally the Jin's turn.
c4_14: The Jin massed a huge army in the mountains near the Great Wall, / at Badger's Mouth.
c4_15: The records say hundreds of thousands, but many historians call that an exaggeration. / What's certain is that they far outnumbered the Mongols.
c4_16: But this position had a weakness.
c4_17: The army was strung out along narrow mountain passes. / No matter how many men they had, only those at the very front / could actually fight.
c4_18: On top of that, a Jin envoy defected to the Mongols, / and gave away the entire Jin deployment.
c4_19: They're still feeding their horses. / Strike now, and they're yours.
c4_20: Genghis Khan massed his forces in one place.
c4_21: General Muqali led a band of men sworn to die / straight into the heart of the Jin army.
c4_22: Cut a long column in the middle, / and the front and back can't help each other. / Their huge numbers had become a burden.
c4_23: The broken Jin army fled down the narrow passes all at once, / trampling one another. / The chronicles say the bodies stretched on for more than thirty miles.
c4_25: Meet a larger enemy on narrow ground, not open plains.
c4_27: Concentrate your force in one place.
c4_28: And chase the broken enemy down.
c4_29: The Mongols would use this formula again and again.
c4_30: The frightened Jin emperor bought peace with a princess, 3,000 horses, and silk. Months later… he abandoned his capital and fled south.
c4_31: We made peace… and you're packing?
c4_32: Genghis Khan saw it as betrayal.
c4_33: In 1215, the Jin capital, Zhongdu, fell. / Today, we call it Beijing.
c5_01: With Zhongdu taken, Genghis Khan left the war with the Jin to General Muqali and turned west, / to the rising power of the Islamic world: the Khwarazmian Empire.
c5_02: What he wanted wasn't war. It was trade.
c5_03: Tell the ruler of the setting sun: / I am the ruler of the rising sun. / Let there be peace between us, and let our merchants come and go freely.
c5_04: In 1218, hundreds of merchants sent by Genghis Khan / led their camels into Otrar, a border city of Khwarazm.
c5_05: Inalchuq, the Khwarazmian governor of that border town, / accused the merchants of spying.
c5_06: And then, / he had them all killed.
c5_07: Genghis Khan was furious. But he couldn't draw his sword just yet. / His army was still at war with the Jin. / So first, he sent envoys to the king of Khwarazm, / demanding the governor who had killed his merchants.
c5_08: But the king of Khwarazm beheaded one envoy, / and shaved the beards of the rest before sending them back.
c5_09: On the steppe, harming an envoy / was the same as declaring war.
c5_10: Now war could not be avoided. / But Khwarazm was an empire several times larger than the Mongols.
c5_17: This war… / was not started by the Mongols. / Heaven, give me the strength to win.
c0_01: This is the start of our Mongol Empire series.
c3_01: In 1206, Genghis Khan brought the tribes of the steppe together. / But yesterday's blood enemies were now one army. / When a battle turned, men scattered after their own chiefs. / For centuries, every steppe army had worked this way.
c5_11: News of the war sent a shiver through the Mongol camp.
c5_12: Khan, if we open a front in the west with the Jin still in the east, / we'll have enemies in front of us and behind us.
c5_13: Khan… if you don't come back, / who will lead this nation?
c5_14: Not even Genghis Khan could be sure he'd come back alive from this war.
c5_15: …If I fight them now, / can I win?
c5_16: Genghis Khan climbed a mountain alone, took off his hat, / and prayed for three days and three nights.
c5_18: At dawn on the third day, Genghis Khan put his hat back on. / There was no doubt left in his face.
c5_19: He came down the mountain, / and ordered the march on Khwarazm.
c5_20: The king of Khwarazm, who had beheaded the envoy, fled from the Mongol horsemen, / escaping by boat to a tiny island.
c5_21: A year later, he died there alone, without even a shroud.
c5_22: So what happened in that one year?
c5_23: The Mongol Empire series continues in Part 2.
